clue.text: Roughly mix lard with egg yolk for a start

indicators.note: to mix the words lard and egg is to stir their letters into a new order
for a start asks for only the opening letter of the word yolk

explanation.surface: A cookery instruction: blend the lard with an egg yolk to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mix' rearranges LARDEGG into RAGGEDL; 'for a start' adds the first letter of 'yolk'. 'Roughly' looks like a cooking adverb but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Done unevenly or crudely, roughly and raggedly are adverbial synonyms.

clue.text: See a sailor about soldiers the French find co-operative

indicators.note: about means the first letters go around the soldier word

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
men are soldiers, as in officers and men
le is the French for the

explanation.surface: Seek out a sailor about some troops the French think helpful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is only a link word; the surface pictures meeting a sailor, but the opening verb gives nothing to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone willing to go along with a plan is agreeable and compliant.

clue.text: Much travelled man has artichoke, say, with pork dish

parts.note: a globe artichoke, so globe is an example given with say
a pig's trotter is a pork dish

explanation.surface: A traveller dines on artichoke and pig's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: A globe is one kind of artichoke; a trotter is a pig's foot cooked as a dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who travels widely around the world is a globetrotter.

clue.text: One of Wordsworth's host's bloomers

parts.note: the poet saw a host of golden flowers; bloomers looks like underwear or blunders but means flowers

explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' sees 'a host, of golden daffodils'. 'host' looks like a person entertaining, and 'bloomers' like gaffes.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellow spring bulb flower celebrated in Wordsworth's famous lyric.

clue.text: Longed for the old composer to be given a note

parts.note: ye is an old form of the
Thomas Arne, English composer of Rule, Britannia
D is a musical note

explanation.surface: The old composer pined to be given a note.
explanation.walkthrough: Arne is the English composer of 'Rule, Britannia!'.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to long or pine for something.

clue.text: Sister-one in a company representing the Holy See?

parts.note: a nun is a religious sister

indicators.note: in means the numeral sits inside the company abbreviation

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A nun, one of a group, acts on behalf of the Vatican.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I inside CO. The definition is phrased loosely: the answer is the one representing the Holy See.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pope's ambassador to a foreign state is a papal envoy.

clue.text: Case required for pianoforte tuition

indicators.note: required for suggests the needed letters lie within the following words

explanation.surface: A case is needed for piano lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'required for' points into 'pianofortE TUItion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small ornamental container for needles and such is an etui.

clue.text: Hot line used to give one's love to the marines

parts.note: I is one, so one's gives I and S
O, the tennis score of zero, is love
taken as written
RM is the Royal Marines

explanation.surface: A hotline is used to send love to the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot line' looks like a telephone link but is a line on a weather map joining places of equal temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: A line on a map joining points of equal temperature, so a temperature line.

clue.text: Return to see about money for schools

indicators.note: about means the turned letters go around the coin word
Return tells us to turn the word see round so it reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a ducat is an old gold coin, a piece of money

explanation.surface: Someone goes back to look at the funding for schools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' makes EES from 'see', and 'about' wraps those letters round DUCAT. 'schools' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or train them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: A day to introduce Prohibition

parts.note: VE Day, Victory in Europe day, gives the letters VE
taken as written

explanation.surface: A date is set on which Prohibition is to come into force.
explanation.walkthrough: VE Day (8 May 1945, Victory in Europe) is a well-known day in Britain. 'introduce' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: A veto is a ban or prohibition imposed by someone with authority.

clue.text: Ordering rich roast beef without a sign of Anno Domini? No!

indicators.note: ordering the letters of rich roast beef means arranging them afresh

parts.note: taken as written: this letter is the one left over

explanation.surface: Someone orders a roast beef dinner with no sign that it was cooked in modern times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordering' rearranges RICHROASTBEEF, and 'without a' says one A is left out of the result. 'sign of' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Years marked BC come before the Christian era, the opposite of those labelled Anno Domini.

clue.text: Renewal of an area, introducing a neater arrangement

indicators.note: introducing means the rearranged letters are put into the area word

parts.note: a region is an area

indicators.note: an arrangement of the word neater shuffles its letters

explanation.surface: An area is renewed by bringing in neater planning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of an area' reads like part of the definition, but 'an area' is the outer piece and only 'Renewal' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Regeneration is revival or restoring something to new life.

clue.text: A flier a man brought down

parts.note: a bat is a flying mammal, so a flier
Ed is a man's name, short for Edward

explanation.surface: A bird and a man were shot down together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought down' suggests shooting the flier, but it is the definition: lessened or reduced.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm that has abated has lessened, been reduced in force.

clue.text: Stretch a point on entrance, accepting a pound

indicators.note: accepting means the other letters take in the pound sign between them

parts.note: E (east) is a point of the compass
taken as written
a gate is an entrance to a field or garden
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: Someone exaggerates at the gate after paying a pound to get in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch a point' is an idiom meaning exaggerate, which misleads; only 'Stretch' defines, and 'a point' is a compass direction.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something is to draw it out, a direct synonym.

clue.text: About to fashion something on a wheel

parts.note: re is a Latin-derived word for about or concerning
to mould is to shape or fashion

explanation.surface: A potter is about to shape something on the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a potter's wheel, but the wheel is a car's: a remould is a retreaded tyre, a common British term.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreaded tyre, fitted to a road vehicle's rim, is called a remould in Britain.

clue.text: Last to restore military strength? No way!

parts.note: to rearm is to supply with weapons again
O is nought, zero, nothing
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A rhetorical question about rearming, rejected out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No way!' looks like an exclamation but supplies O and ST.
explanation.definitionFit: The one at the very back, furthest behind, is rearmost.

clue.text: "She was a of delight" (Wordsworth)

parts.note: a gap in a quotation: the missing word completes the opening line of a Wordsworth poem about a lovely spirit

explanation.walkthrough: The opening line of Wordsworth's poem is 'She was a Phantom of delight'; the clue asks for the word in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem calls the woman an apparition or spirit, a vision of delight.

clue.text: Impeded boy carrying basket of goodies

indicators.note: carrying here puts the boy piece after, as if hauling the basket along behind

parts.note: a hamper is a basket of food and treats
Ed is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy is weighed down carrying a basket of treats.
explanation.walkthrough: A hamper is a wicker basket of food, a common British Christmas gift. 'carrying' joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampered means hindered or obstructed, a synonym of impeded.

clue.text: Sadly I got a bill (with a pound rebate) for essential parts

indicators.note: sadly shows the letters of I got a bill are disordered

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone is sad to get a bill, though a pound comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' rearranges IGOTABILL; 'rebate' takes one L out. Musically, obligati are parts that must be played.
explanation.definitionFit: In music an obligato is an accompaniment that must not be omitted, so an indispensable part.

clue.text: Joint international giving protective covering

parts.note: the knee is a joint
a cap is awarded to an international player in sport

explanation.surface: A joint international match brings protective clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a player picked for the national side wins a cap, so 'international' gives CAP.
explanation.definitionFit: The patella is the bony plate shielding the front of the knee.

clue.text: No aside for a digger in the National

indicators.note: No here means the following letters are left out of the word

parts.note: a digger is Australian slang for an Australian soldier or citizen
read as a side: A plus L, the left side

explanation.surface: Someone in the Grand National is told there is no place for an Australian.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'aside' as 'a side', A + L (left); 'No' removes those from AUSTRALIAN. 'Digger' is a nickname for an Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Austria is a national of that country.

clue.text: One representative to publicise damage

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
an MP, Member of Parliament, is a representative
to air a view is to publicise it

explanation.surface: A single MP goes public to do harm.
explanation.walkthrough: MP is a Member of Parliament, an elected representative.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair is to weaken or harm.

clue.text: Rock Alley

definitions.meaning: a metamorphic stone used in sculpture
a large glass playing ... in a children's game

explanation.definitionFit: Both a polished stone used by sculptors and a glass ball used as a taw in children's games.

clue.text: Terrible miser with a gift to deceive

indicators.note: terrible here shows the word miser is badly mangled into a new order

parts.note: a present is a gift

explanation.surface: A horrid miser hands over a gift with intent to cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' looks like a description of the miser, but it is the anagram signal; 'with' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a false account of something is to deceive by misleading statements.

clue.text: Money problems at school

definitions.meaning: ... of money are amounts of it

explanation.definitionFit: Both amounts of cash and arithmetic exercises set in class.

clue.text: One leading form of transport was terrible

indicators.note: leading means the first piece goes in front of the second

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a van is a form of road transport

explanation.surface: A man at the front of a vehicle was dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the Russian tsar known as the Terrible.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia's sixteenth-century tsar is known to history by the epithet 'the Terrible'.

clue.text: A lemon one's cut up for this pudding

indicators.note: cut up suggests the letters are chopped and rearranged

parts.note: I is one, so one's gives I and S

explanation.surface: A lemon is chopped for a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut up' rearranges ALEMON + IS. A dessert of milky semolina is a classic British school dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse wheat meal cooked with milk makes a well-known milk pudding.

clue.text: Starts to put Elsie down as not the ideal companion, being so finicky

indicators.note: starts to asks for the opening letter of each of the next three words

parts.note: an antic is a clown or buffoon, not someone you would choose to spend time with

explanation.surface: Someone takes against Elsie as a companion, being so fussy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' takes the first letters of 'put', 'Elsie', 'down'. The printed clue spells the definition 'finnicky'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fussy over small details and rules is pedantic, a close synonym.
